HowWeRank.title: How we rank
HowWeRank.intro: The ranking is a transparent weighted average. You choose the weights, we do the arithmetic. It tells you which resorts fit your priorities, never which terrain is safe.
HowWeRank.formulaBody: Every factor is first converted to a value between 0 (worst resort in our list) and 1 (best resort) by min-max scaling across all resorts. Filters never change the scores, they only hide resorts. Price is inverted, so the cheapest resort gets 1. If all resorts have the same value for a factor, it counts as a neutral 0.5.

measures.terrain: Our editorial rating from 1 to 5 for how varied the off-piste terrain is.
measures.vertical: Vertical drop in metres between the highest lift and the base.
measures.snowfall: Average November to April snowfall at summit elevation over the winters 2015/16 to 2024/25, from the ERA5 reanalysis via Open-Meteo.
measures.altitude: Average of top and base elevation, as a proxy for snow reliability.
measures.steepness: Upper end of the typical off-piste steepness range, in degrees.
measures.liftAccess: Number of lift-accessed freeride areas we list for the resort.
measures.price: Midpoint of the typical day-pass price range. Cheaper scores higher.
measures.conditions: Fresh snow in the last 72 hours from the Open-Meteo forecast model. Skipped whenever live data is unavailable: sample data is never used for ranking.
measures.safety: Half for freeride guides being available, half for beginner-friendly off-piste.

HowWeRank.missingBody: If a factor has no data for a resort, it is left out of that resort's average instead of counting as zero.
HowWeRank.safetyTitle: What the safety slider does and does not do
HowWeRank.safetyBody: The safety factor only rewards resorts where guides are available and where beginner-friendly off-piste exists. It does not rate how dangerous a mountain is, and a high rank never means the terrain is safe. Avalanche danger changes daily: always read the official bulletin for the region.
limits: Terrain variety and the beginner flag are editorial judgements, not measurements.
Elevations, prices and steepness are approximate estimates that we have not yet verified against official sources.
ERA5 is a coarse (about 25 km) reanalysis. Snowfall values are good for comparing resorts, not for predicting a specific day.
The same November to April window is used for every resort, so late-season resorts such as Riksgränsen are under-counted.

Safety.title: Safety
Safety.intro: Free tools to prepare for off-piste skiing. They support, but never replace, an avalanche course with a qualified instructor, the official bulletin and your own judgement on the day.
Safety.notSubstitute: For education only. This is not a substitute for an avalanche course, a qualified guide, the official avalanche bulletin or your own judgement on the day.

Safety.dangerIntro: The European avalanche danger scale (EAWS) used by the official bulletins. Most avalanche accidents happen at levels 2 (Moderate) and 3 (Considerable). Always read the full bulletin for your region.

dangerMeaning.1: Generally favourable. Triggering is possible only from a high additional load, on a few very steep slopes.
dangerMeaning.2: The snowpack is weak on some steep slopes and stable elsewhere. Triggering is possible mainly from a high additional load, on the slopes named in the bulletin.
dangerMeaning.3: Dangerous conditions. Triggering is possible even from a low additional load, such as a single skier, especially on the steep slopes named in the bulletin.
dangerMeaning.4: Dangerous conditions. Triggering is likely even from a low additional load on many steep slopes. Natural avalanches are likely.
dangerMeaning.5: Very dangerous conditions. Many large natural avalanches are expected, even on moderately steep terrain.

Safety.learnBody: Take an avalanche course with a qualified instructor and practise rescue with your group every season. Good starting points:
Safety.learnSlf: SLF (WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research): avalanche information
Safety.learnIcar: ICAR, the International Commission for Alpine Rescue

Checklist.title: Gear and trip checklist
Checklist.intro: Tick things off as you go. Your list is saved on this device only, and you can print it.
Checklist.storageNote: Your ticks are stored in this browser. If storage is blocked, the list still works but is not remembered.

transceiver.label: Avalanche transceiver (beacon)
transceiver.hint: Fresh batteries, worn under your outer layer, switched on and in send mode.

probe.label: Avalanche probe
probe.hint: At least 240 cm long. Assemble it and test it before you go.

shovel.label: Avalanche shovel
shovel.hint: A metal blade. Plastic blades can break in hard snow.

airbag.label: Avalanche airbag pack (recommended)
airbag.hint: Check the cartridge or canister, the handle and the pack before every trip.

helmet.label: Helmet
helmet.hint: For falls and for trees and rocks.

firstaid.label: First-aid kit and emergency blanket
firstaid.hint: Know how to use what is in it.

phone.label: Charged phone with the emergency number saved
phone.hint: 112 works across Europe. Also save the local mountain rescue number.

headlamp.label: Headlamp and spare batteries
headlamp.hint: Days are short and trips take longer than planned.

navigation.label: Map, compass or offline navigation
navigation.hint: Do not rely on a single phone in the cold.

clothing.label: Spare warm layer, gloves, goggles and sun protection

bulletin.label: Read the official avalanche bulletin for your region
bulletin.hint: Check the danger level, the aspects and elevations, and the avalanche problems.

weather.label: Check the weather and wind forecast
weather.hint: Fresh snow and strong wind change the avalanche danger quickly.

route.label: Plan a route that fits the conditions and your group
route.hint: When the danger is high, choose gentler terrain with no steep slopes above you.

inform.label: Tell someone your route and when you will be back

skills.label: Make sure everyone can use their rescue gear
skills.hint: Practise searching with your transceiver regularly, not only once.

daylight.label: Plan for daylight and set a turn-around time

groupcheck.label: Do a transceiver check with the whole group
groupcheck.hint: Everyone in send mode, one person in search mode checks every device, then everyone switches back to send.

airbagcheck.label: Check that airbag packs are armed

agree.label: Agree on the plan, the rules and who does what
agree.hint: Spacing, one at a time on steep slopes, where to regroup, and who leads the rescue.

signs.label: Watch for warning signs along the way
signs.hint: Recent avalanches, whumpfing sounds, cracks shooting out from your skis, fresh wind-blown snow.

Aspects.title: Slope aspect and steepness
Aspects.intro: Two things decide where avalanches can happen: which way a slope faces (its aspect) and how steep it is. Try the tools below.
Aspects.aspectTitle: Aspect: which way does a slope face?
Aspects.aspectHelp: Aspect is the compass direction a slope faces, the direction you look when you face downhill. Choose a direction on the compass to see what it means.
Aspects.modeLabel: What do you want to explore?
Aspects.modeAspect: Sun and snow on each aspect
Aspects.modeWind: Where does wind load the snow?

aspectInfo.N: North-facing slopes get the least sun in winter. Snow stays cold and powdery longer, and weak layers can survive longer in the snowpack.
aspectInfo.NE: North-east-facing slopes get little sun, mostly in the morning. Like north, they keep cold snow, and weak layers can persist.
aspectInfo.E: East-facing slopes get the morning sun. Snow warms up earlier in the day, especially in spring.
aspectInfo.SE: South-east-facing slopes get strong morning sun. Snow warms early, and wet-snow avalanches become more likely on sunny spring days.
aspectInfo.S: South-facing slopes get the most sun. Snow warms quickly, and wet-snow and gliding-snow avalanches are more likely in sunny weather.
aspectInfo.SW: South-west-facing slopes get strong afternoon sun. The warmest time is later in the day, when wet-snow avalanches become more likely in spring.
aspectInfo.W: West-facing slopes get the afternoon sun. Whether wind loads them depends on the wind direction on the day.
aspectInfo.NW: North-west-facing slopes get little sun, mostly late in the day. Like north, they keep cold snow, and weak layers can persist.

Aspects.windResult: Wind from {from}: snow is blown over the ridge and mostly deposited on the sheltered (lee) side, on slopes facing {lee}. Slopes facing across the wind can be loaded too. Wind slabs can form within hours and often look smooth and pillow-like.
Aspects.leeLegend: Highlighted: most likely to be loaded
Aspects.steepnessHelp: Move the slider to see how steep a slope is and what it means for avalanches.

flat.title: Under 25°: gentle
flat.body: Slab avalanches rarely release here. But check the terrain above you: avalanches from steeper slopes can run out onto gentle ground.

borderline.title: 25–29°: borderline
borderline.body: Avalanches are uncommon but possible, for example when the danger is high or the snow is wet or gliding.

terrain.title: 30–34°: avalanche terrain
terrain.body: Dry slab avalanches can release. This is where the warnings in the bulletin start to apply.

peak.title: 35–39°: the most common accident range
peak.body: Most avalanche accidents happen on slopes of about 35–40°.

steep.title: 40–45°: steep avalanche terrain
steep.body: Still avalanche terrain. Slides can be fast and falls serious.

verysteep.title: Over 45°: very steep
verysteep.body: Snow sheds in small slides more often, so deep slabs are less common. But sluffs, falls and cliffs are serious hazards. This is expert terrain.

whyBody: Below about 30° a slope is usually not steep enough for a slab to slide, even when a weak layer is present.
Between about 30° and 45° snow can build a cohesive slab on a weak layer, and the slope is steep enough for the slab to slide. This is where most slab avalanche accidents happen.
Above 45° snow tends to shed in small slides as it falls, so thick slabs build up less often. That does not make it safe: falls and sluffs are serious in their own right.
Aspects.whyNote: These are rules of thumb, not a safe/unsafe switch. Avalanches can start outside this range, and an avalanche from a steep slope can run out onto gentle ground below.
Aspects.measureBody: Use a slope-angle card, an inclinometer or a phone app, and measure the steepest part of the slope. Slope maps and the aspects and elevations in the bulletin help you plan before you go.
Aspects.bulletinBody: The bulletin tells you which aspects and elevations are most dangerous today. Combine that with the steepness of the slopes on your route and choose terrain that fits the conditions.

Quiz.title: Avalanche safety quiz
Quiz.intro: 13 questions. Choose one answer for each, then check your answers. It is a way to learn, not training: take an avalanche course and practise rescue with your group.
Quiz.unanswered: {count, plural, one {# question was not answered and counts as wrong.} other {# questions were not answered and count as wrong.}}

verdict.high: Great result. Keep your knowledge fresh and keep practising rescue.
verdict.mid: A good start. Read the explanations and revisit the topics you missed.
verdict.low: There is plenty to learn. Read the explanations, and consider an avalanche course before going off-piste.

q1.question: Which three items make up the essential avalanche rescue kit that everyone off-piste should carry and know how to use?
q1.explanation: A transceiver finds a buried person, a probe pinpoints them and a shovel gets them out. Everyone in the group needs all three and must practise using them.

q2.question: What does danger level 3, "Considerable", mean?
options: Triggering is possible even from a single skier, especially on the steep slopes named in the bulletin
Many large avalanches are expected even on gentle terrain
q2.explanation: At level 3 the snowpack is only moderately to weakly bonded on many steep slopes, so a low additional load can be enough. Many accidents happen at levels 2 and 3.

q3.question: On which slope angles do most slab avalanche accidents happen?
q3.explanation: Slabs mostly release on slopes steeper than about 30°, and accidents peak around 35–40°. Above about 45° snow sheds more often in small slides.

q4.question: A strong wind blows from the west. Which slopes are most likely to be loaded with fresh wind slabs?
options: East-facing slopes, on the sheltered side
q4.explanation: Wind carries snow over the ridge and drops it on the sheltered (lee) side. Slopes across the wind can be cross-loaded as well.

q5.question: What is a terrain trap?
options: A gully, creek bed or depression where even a small avalanche can bury someone deeply
q5.explanation: In a gully or hollow, snow piles up deeply, so even a small avalanche can have serious consequences. Trees, cliffs and lake edges can be traps too.

q6.question: A friend has been buried by an avalanche. What is the best first action?
options: Ski down to get help and leave the scene
Wait for the rescue team to arrive
Switch your transceiver to search and start the search straight away, while someone else calls the emergency services
Start digging in the middle of the avalanche
q6.explanation: Survival chances fall quickly with time, and companions are the only help that arrives fast enough. Search immediately; if someone else can call 112 at the same time, do that.

q7.question: After roughly how long do the survival chances of a completely buried person start to fall sharply?
options: They do not change with time
q7.explanation: Chances are best in the first minutes and fall quickly after about 15 minutes. This is why a fast companion rescue matters so much.

q8.question: On this site a region shows "No current data". What should you do?
options: Use the level from last week
Read the official bulletin of the local warning service before you go, and do not go without that information
Ask for opinions on social media
q8.explanation: "No current data" means we have no up-to-date bulletin to show you, not that the danger is low. Only the current official bulletin can tell you the danger.

q9.question: Which of these is a clear warning sign of unstable snow?
options: Whumpfing sounds or cracks that shoot out from your skis
Many other people on the slope
q9.explanation: A whumpf means a weak layer has collapsed, and shooting cracks show that a slab is connected over a wide area. Both are strong signs to leave the slope.

q10.question: What is the best way for a group to cross a steep slope?
options: Bunched up so nobody gets lost
The most experienced person last, out of sight
One at a time, with the others watching from a safe spot
q10.explanation: One at a time limits how many people can be caught, and the others can watch, and start a rescue, from safety. Keep spacing and regroup at safe places.

q11.question: Which statement about airbag packs is true?
options: They can reduce the risk of burial but do not replace the transceiver, probe and shovel, or training
They only work on snow-covered roads
q11.explanation: An airbag can lower the chance of being buried, but it does not always work and does not protect against trauma. Always carry the full rescue kit as well.

q12.question: A bulletin lists the problem "persistent weak layers". What does it mean for your plans?
options: The danger is lower than usual
Avalanches can release days after snowfall and be hard to predict, so you should choose terrain very conservatively
q12.explanation: A persistent weak layer can stay in the snowpack for weeks. Slabs may release later, from a distance or on a slope that was skied safely before, so keep to gentle terrain.

q13.question: A bulletin says "Considerable above 2,200 m, aspects north to east". What does this mean?
options: The whole region is at level 3
The danger is highest on slopes facing north to east above 2,200 m, so avoid them or be extremely conservative
The danger applies only below 2,200 m
The danger applies only at night
q13.explanation: Bulletins name the aspects and elevations that are most dangerous. Read them carefully and combine them with the steepness of the slopes on your route.
